concept.name: Best execution
concept.definition: The regulatory and fiduciary duty of a broker-dealer to seek the most favorable terms reasonably available for a customer's order under the circumstances - weighing price, speed, likelihood of execution and settlement, size, and nature of the order - rather than simply the nominal best price. In the U.S. it is embedded in FINRA Rule 5310 and antifraud principles; in the EU in MiFID II Article 27.
concept.intuition: Your broker must work your order as a loyal agent would: not necessarily the single best tick, but the best overall outcome reasonably achievable for that order.
concept.mechanics: Firms must establish policies and conduct 'regular and rigorous' reviews of execution quality across venues, considering price improvement opportunities, speed, and fill likelihood; routing decisions driven by payment for order flow must still satisfy the duty. Execution quality is evidenced through Rule 605 statistics and firm-level venue analysis.
concept.failure_modes: The duty is process-based, not outcome-based, so it can be technically satisfied while routing to mediocre venues; conflicts from payment for order flow and affiliated venues are the persistent weak point. Defining 'best' across speed/price/certainty trade-offs is genuinely judgment-laden.
concept.misconceptions: Best execution does not mean the best possible price on every trade - speed and certainty legitimately trade off against price, and the standard is 'reasonably available' terms. Nor is it satisfied by default routing: periodic, documented venue review is required.
concept.example: A broker routes a retail market order to a wholesaler offering consistent sub-penny price improvement and fast fills, and documents quarterly reviews comparing those statistics against exchange execution quality - evidencing best execution compliance.
